anti_generic_signature_read: Asked what stops this being an off-the-shelf version of whatever it is: 'The strongest thing by a wide margin is the cyan planet's attitude. The ring runs pole-over-pole, near vertical, while in the same set the yellow ringed planet has its ring around its waist in the ordinary way. Whoever made this did not reuse the ring part. Then the polar view closes the argument: looking down what would be the SIDE of an ordinary planet, you get a ring that is perfectly face-on, a circle, with the grey cap sitting dead centre inside it. That is a correct, non-obvious, physically meaningful depiction of an axial tilt lying in the orbital plane, and it is expressed purely in geometry -- no text, no arrow, no diagram. Someone who has never heard the fact could pick up two pieces and SEE it.'
blind_action_read: 'Nothing in these images has a moving mechanism. No hinge, no pivot, no latch, no gear, no slide, no living hinge, no clip, no threaded joint. I have looked for a parting line on the pedestals and on the board and found none. What the object clearly invites is handling rather than mechanism: the pieces are separate from the board and stand loose on it, so they are picked up and moved from cell to cell.' That is the correct read: nothing in this set moves against anything else, and motion is not claimed.
blind_form_read: 'The board slab: flat. A rectangular plate with visible thickness. The grid: cut INTO the top surface, narrow V- or U-channels scribed down into the plate, not raised walls. The terrain cells: a mixture of both -- the brown cells each have a large round dish cut down into the cell, and standing around the rim a ring of small pyramidal bumps that stand proud. The pedestals: round, a squat cylinder, a disc puck, its top edge carrying a small rounded-over lip. The planet bodies: fully round, true spheres. The ring on the cyan planet: a thin flat annulus standing proud of the sphere, a separate hoop. The polar cap: a grey disc ON the sphere, and it follows the sphere's curvature -- the shading gradient is spherical, not flat, so it is a surface region rather than a flat sticker. It is flush; I see no step at its edge, only a hard colour boundary.'
blind_held_read: Unprompted, before anything was revealed: 'A two-player tabletop board game (or teaching set) about the solar system: a thick gridded slab board, sixteen sphere-on-pedestal playing pieces split into a white-footed set and a black-footed set, and two flat trays with scooped pockets to stow the pieces in.' It reached that from the images alone -- 'the pedestals come in precisely two finishes, white and black, and I can count eight of each, which is the classic signature of a two-side game rather than a display model' -- and flagged its own uncertainty honestly: 'I see no dice, cards, score track, or printed rules in any image.'
blind_relationship_read: 'The board is the ground plane and everything is referred to it: one piece to one cell, footprint sized so a pedestal sits comfortably inside a single square. Within a single piece the hierarchy is clear: the pedestal carries the planet. It is the only load path. The ring is carried by the planet, and in the cyan piece's case it is carried down into the pedestal -- so the ring is not merely orbiting the ball in free space; it is anchored, and the pedestal is doing structural duty for it. The two colour families relate to each other by opposition: same geometry, same ring, same cap. So foot colour is the only thing distinguishing the two sets -- ownership, not species.'
blind_subjects_read: Named unprompted, planet by planet, with the image it was named from: 'Uranus -- I say Uranus specifically, not just a ringed planet, because of three things together: the flat cyan-green colour, a ring system standing VERTICALLY rather than around the waist, and a polar cap that faces sideways. That combination is Uranus's ~98 degree axial tilt, and nothing else in the sky looks like it.' Also Neptune ('deep blue, white streaked cloud bands, and a dark grey oval'), Jupiter ('orange-cream horizontal banding, and a small red-orange oval reading as the Great Red Spot'), Saturn ('pale yellow globe with a broad ring around its waist, tilted a modest amount -- the ordinary, expected ring attitude'), Earth, Mars, and probably Venus and Mercury. 'Eight distinct planet types, present twice each. Sixteen pieces total.'

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1, unprompted and before anything was revealed, the critic named the feature as a polar cap without being given the word: 'a polar cap that faces sideways -- out at the viewer in the 3/4 views', and used it as one of three cues to identify the planet as Uranus. In round 3 it measured the cap at 262 px across a 574 px ball and described it as 'a pale oval', never as a band or a stripe. No round described any belt of latitude on this piece.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The equatorial band is replaced by a POLAR HOOD -- a broad region around the pole, not a belt of latitude.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1, describing the cap's edge without prompting: 'It is flush; I see no step at its edge, only a hard colour boundary.' Round 3 described it as 'hard-edged' with a clean elliptical outline and listed no lobe, scallop or rim structure in any of the three rounds.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The hood has NO lobed or scalloped rim; its boundary is a plain closed curve.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1 read the cap on the cyan piece on the white base and on the cyan piece on the black base, and confirmed from the pair frame that both carry it: 'the identical cyan planet on a white puck and on a black puck, same geometry, same ring, same cap.' Round 3 located the cap on both board pieces at ~x 765 y 225 and ~x 790 y 710.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The hood is visible on BOTH armies at the frames the set is photographed from.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1 described the only encircling feature on the piece as running 'pole-over-pole, near vertical', explicitly contrasting it with the other ringed planet's waist ring. Round 3, asked directly whether any piece reads as painted stripes, answered no for every piece on the board and described the cyan piece as 'a cyan ball with a subtle darker-cyan arc that reads as a seam or moulding line in the material, plus a pale oval'.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: There is NO equatorial stripe anywhere on the cyan globe.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1 read the tilt off the geometry unprompted and called it correct: 'a correct, non-obvious, physically meaningful depiction of an axial tilt lying in the orbital plane', identifying it as '~98 degrees' from the images alone. Round 3 confirmed the mirroring survives: the two pieces differ only in base colour.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The 97.77 degree obliquity has not moved; the globe still leans at the planet's true axial tilt, mirrored between armies.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 3, asked the two halves separately against the reference photograph: 'Closer, clearly closer -- and the marking has not vanished.' On the ring: 'the piece has moved from different material to same material, tonal step, which is the KIND of marking the reference uses.' On visibility: 'Image 5 shows a complete, distinct annulus with clear edges. Image 3 shows a clear arc breaking the silhouette. Someone would notice it.'

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1, unprompted: 'the ring runs pole-over-pole, near vertical, while in the same set the yellow ringed planet has its ring around its waist in the ordinary way.' Round 3 confirmed it still reads as a physical hoop after the recolour: 'it still breaks the ball's outline at the top -- a cyan arc standing against the background, which no surface marking can do' and 'shows two distinct faces across its width'.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1, on the load path: 'The ring is carried by the planet, and in the cyan piece's case it is carried down into the pedestal... so the ring is not merely orbiting the ball in free space; it is anchored.' Round 3 saw it as 'a complete annulus' in the polar view with no gap reported at any azimuth in any round.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1 separated them unprompted and used one to identify the other: Saturn has 'the ordinary, expected ring attitude, which is exactly what makes the cyan planet's vertical ring register as deliberate'. Round 3: 'Separation from the two yellow ringed pieces is still trivial -- they have broad pale grey rings standing well clear of yellow banded bodies; these have narrow vertical self-coloured ones.'

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1 named them as two different planets from the side-by-side frame without being told there were two: Neptune from 'the deep-blue-plus-white-streaks combination distinguishing it from the cyan piece beside it', Uranus from its colour, ring attitude and cap. Round 3 re-read the same frame and again separated them.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The piece stays distinguishable from Neptune, the adjacent rank in the blue family.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Round 1, from the pair frame: 'the identical cyan planet on a white puck and on a black puck, same geometry, same ring, same cap. So foot colour is the only thing distinguishing the two sets.' Round 3 settled the one asymmetry it had suspected by measurement and retracted it: cropping the two base nubs and mirroring one, 'the cyan pixel counts are 4462 and 4462 -- exactly identical, and the shapes superimpose', adding 'please record that as my error rather than as something you fixed'.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Verified by the critic against its own saved crops rather than asserted. Round 2: 'Both yellow ringed pieces: bit-identical. critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Across all three rounds the critic's inventory of the cyan piece is exactly ball, cap, one hoop and pedestal. Round 3 listed the piece's features as 'a cyan ball with a subtle darker-cyan arc... plus a pale oval' and nothing else. No moon, storm, band, gap or second ring was reported on this piece in any round.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Nothing is added beyond the polar hood and the one ring: no moons, no storms, no banding, no shepherd gaps, no separate ringlets.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: This is the requirement the correction exists for, and it failed twice before it passed. Rounds 1 and 2 both named the two cyan pieces as tennis balls, round 2 giving the mechanism: 'a bold white curved line arcing down one side of a saturated-colour ball, and a large pale panel on the opposite side'. After the ring was moved into the globe's own filament, round 3 answered: 'No. It is no longer a tennis ball... a cyan ball with a subtle darker-cyan arc that reads as a seam or moulding line in the material, plus a pale oval. That is not a tennis ball. I checked the other pieces too -- the blue streaked ones read as cloud bands, the banded orange ones as bands, the small grey ones carry a single pit. None reads as painted stripes.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NO piece anywhere on the board reads as a beach ball or a tennis ball.

largest_risk: The critic's, in its own words and not softened. With the ring quietened, the polar hood is the only high-contrast marking left on the piece, and it is the one feature that has no counterpart in the reference photograph at all: 'the pale oval is now the only high-contrast marking on the piece, it is still hard-edged and flush, and it sits off to one side. At board scale it now reads to me as a stuck-on disc or, mildly, an eye. The tennis ball is genuinely gone; a weaker misread has inherited the space it left.' Narrowing the hood from 55 to 60 degrees of latitude took it from about a third of the visible face to about a fifth and did not change that character, because a flush colour inlay has a hard edge and cannot fade out. Behind it sits the thing no choice in this correction could reach: the globe prints in `cyan` #00FFFF, saturation 1.00, and the reference is a pale desaturated ice blue at saturation 0.22. The critic named that as the largest remaining gap: 'If the goal is to approach the reference, the body saturation and the cap are where the remaining distance is.' The Wish fixes the cyan globe and mandates the hood, so neither was available to this run; both are recorded in the product limitations, and a pale blue filament is recommended there for a future revision rather than acted on here. The ring-to-base junction is the third item: the critic read it as 'sawn off' rather than supported in all three rounds. It is a sound joint -- one solid, 0 bridges, the overhang gate passing at 44.3 degrees against 45 -- and it is not a handsome one.
resolution: Three review rounds, two focused repairs, one independent critic, geometry and images regenerated in full before each re-review. Round 1 was unprimed and identified the object, named Uranus from its tilt alone, and answered the correction's own decisive question -- does any piece still read as a beach ball or a tennis ball -- with yes, naming both cyan pieces. Repair 1 took the ring from `white` to `gray`; round 2 measured the change, credited it as astronomically right, and reported the tennis ball still present and the darker line if anything a MORE convincing seam, because a tennis seam is a dark curve on a bright ball. That result is what identified the real mechanism: the painted-stripe reading did not live in how far the ring's tone sat from the globe -- `white` measured 38.9 luma levels away and `gray` 7.0, and both produced it -- but in the ring being a different MATERIAL from the ball. Repair 2 moved the ring into the globe's own `cyan` and narrowed the hood from 55 to 60 degrees. Round 3 reported the tennis ball gone, the ring still legible as a hoop up close and still tellable from Saturn's at board scale, and the piece measurably closer to its reference; it also retracted two of its own earlier findings once it measured them, and caught one genuine error of this run's -- a stale render left in the image set -- which was regenerated. One review round of the allowance remains unused. Motion is not verified and is not claimed: the operator's `check_motion` is false for this run and nothing in this set moves against anything else. No print-readiness is claimed: `print_gate_sha256s` is deliberately empty and the product seals as `digitally-verified-not-print-ready`.
reviewer: One independent native critic, three rounds, shown only the renders and no other file. Round 1 was fully unprimed; rounds 2 and 3 are disclosed re-reviews after a repair, not naive reads.
